Kedāranātha
------------------------------------------
Most of the Hindu पिल्ग्रिमगे centres are situated in places where nature’s beauty automatically induces peace and joy in the hearts of the devout pilgrims. Among these, the Himālayan centres like बदरीनाथ and केदारनाथ (also spelt as ‘Kedārnāth’), stand supreme.
Kedāranātha is actually a very small town—almost like a hamlet—and is famous because of the ancient शिव temple. It is one of the twelve ज्योतिर्लिङ्गस् (liṅgas full of divine effulgence). The story goes that it was built by the Pāṇḍavas to atone for the sin of killing their cousins and others in the कुरुक्षेत्र war.
Kedārnātha TempleIt is located in the Garhwal district of Uttaranchal, at a height of 3600 metres (11,760 ft.) above the sea-level.
The लिङ्ग in the गर्भगृह or sanctum is of an irregular shape, 3.6 metres (12 ft.) in circumference at the bottom and 0.6 metre (2 ft.) in height.
In front of the sanctum there is a मण्डप (hall), a large image of नन्दि (bull, mount of Lord शिव) and also many images of gods and goddesses, including those of the Pāṇḍavas. A light is always kept burning in the sanctum.
The worship is simple and there is no अभिषेक or bathing of the लिङ्ग with water.
The devotees generally offer balls of ghee and are also permitted to embrace the icon.
The priests of the temple are gosains belonging to the लिङ्गायत सेच्त्.
The temple is opened on the अक्षय्य-तृतीया day (in April-May) and is closed the day after दीपावली (November). During the winter months, the उत्सवमूर्ति (processional image) is taken to the place called Ukhimaṭh and the worship continued.
The temple structure is very beautiful. The roof is very high. The river Mandākinī (a tributary of गङ्गा) flows at the back of the temple.
There are five temples in the nearby area. They are: Badarī-kedāra, Madhya-महेश्वर, Tuṅganātha, Rudranātha and Kalleśvara. All these together are called ‘Pañcakedāra’.
At the back of the main temple there is a shrine of शङ्कर (A.

-820). He is said to have disappeared into a cave here.
According to some legends, the first teacher of the Liṅgāyata or the Vīraśaiva sect, Ekorāmārādhya, had his मठ (monastery) here.
See also BADARĪNĀTHA.
